column1: Roughly how many tokens is a word of English text, and what changed with Claude Opus 4.7?
column2: Classic rule: 1 token ≈ 4 characters ≈ 0.75 words. Claude Opus 4.7 and later use a newer tokenizer that produces about 30% more tokens for the same text (1M tokens ≈ 555k words).

column1: What counts toward a Claude model's context window?
column2: Everything in the request (system prompt, all messages including tool results/images/documents, tool definitions) plus the output generated for that turn, including thinking.

column1: How are thinking tokens billed?
column2: As output tokens, once, when they are generated. They are part of max_tokens and count toward rate limits.

column1: What's the cost formula for a single LLM call (no caching or batch)?
column2: input_tokens × input_price / 1M + output_tokens × output_price / 1M. Output is usually priced about 5x higher than input.

column1: How do you know a request's real token usage before vs after sending it?
column2: Before: call the free token-counting endpoint (client.messages.count_tokens) for input tokens. After: read response.usage (input_tokens, output_tokens, cache fields), which is what you're billed on.

column1: What belongs in the system prompt versus the user message?
column2: System prompt: stable rules such as role, output format and what to do when unsure. User message: the per-request input (the document, question or ticket). Both count toward the context window and are billed as input tokens.

column1: Why wrap parts of a prompt in XML-style tags like `<document>` and `<example>`?
column2: It removes ambiguity about where instructions, examples and data begin and end, and lets you ask for output in tags you can parse. It reduces confusion between data and instructions, but is not a security boundary against prompt injection.

column1: How many examples should a few-shot prompt have, and what should they look like?
column2: Typically 3–5, varied: include an edge case and a "none of the above" case. Otherwise the model copies the surface pattern of the examples.

column1: What is the cheapest prompt-level defence against hallucination?
column2: Give an explicit exit, for example "If the answer isn't in the document, reply `not found`", so the model doesn't fill gaps with a confident guess.

column1: Which old prompting habits can you usually drop with modern models?
column2: Grand persona openers ("world's best expert"), ALL-CAPS shouting, emotional pleas or tip promises, and a reflexive "think step by step" when using a reasoning model. Test each on your own examples before keeping it.

column1: What is the model ID and the standard API price of GPT-6.1 Sol?
column2: `gpt-6.1-sol`: $2 per 1M input tokens, $0.10 per 1M cached input tokens, $10 per 1M output tokens. It was released on 2026-09-29.

column1: Where does GPT-6.1 Sol sit in the GPT-6 lineup, and what does OpenAI claim about it?
column2: It is the mid-tier between Astra (flagship) and Luna (small). OpenAI says it nearly matches Astra on agentic coding, computer use and professional work at one-fifth of Astra's token prices (vendor-reported).

column1: Which `reasoning.effort` values does GPT-6.1 Sol accept, and what is the default?
column2: `low`, `medium` (default), `high`, `xhigh` and `max`. `none` and `minimal` are not supported, so code that relied on them should map to `low` and be re-tested.

column1: How do you call GPT-6.1 Sol with tools (function calling)?
column2: Use the Responses API. Chat Completions works only for requests without tools on this model.

column1: Why is reasoning effort a cost dial, and what does `configuration_update` do?
column2: Reasoning tokens are billed as output tokens (5x the input rate here), so higher effort costs more and takes longer. A `configuration_update` input item changes effort mid-conversation without rewriting the prompt prefix, which keeps the cache valid.

column1: In the Responses API, where do you read how many tokens the model spent on reasoning?
column2: `response.usage.output_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens`. Those tokens are part of `output_tokens` and are billed at the output rate.

column1: How do you compute the dollar cost of one call from `usage` when some input was cached?
column2: `((input_tokens − cached_tokens) × input_price + cached_tokens × cached_price + output_tokens × output_price) / 1M`, where `cached_tokens` comes from `usage.input_tokens_details`.

column1: What happens if a reasoning model hits `max_output_tokens`, and why does it matter for evals?
column2: The response has `status="incomplete"` with `incomplete_details.reason="max_output_tokens"`. Reasoning tokens count toward the cap, so a low cap can leave you with little or no visible text. That makes a correct model look wrong.

column1: What is a minimal LLM eval?
column2: A fixed set of inputs with known right answers, graded mechanically (for example by parsing a tagged label), re-run whenever the model, prompt or settings change.

column1: Why change only `reasoning.effort` between runs in an effort benchmark?
column2: So any difference in accuracy, tokens, cost or latency can be attributed to the one variable you changed.

column1: What are Claude Haiku 5.5's API prices per 1M input / output tokens, and where does the price change?
column2: $0.10 / $0.50 for requests of 100,000 tokens or fewer. Above 100k tokens it is $0.50 / $2.50. Haiku 4.5 was $1 / $5. It was released on 2026-10-07.

column1: Why does Anthropic estimate about 75% savings over Haiku 4.5 when per-token prices fell 90%?
column2: Haiku 5.5 reportedly consumes more tokens per task, and some requests land in the pricier long tier. Cost per task is price per token × tokens used, so measure it on your own workload.

column1: How can you reduce cost when a task would push a request past the 100k-token tier?
column2: Split it into smaller requests that each stay under 100k (map), then combine the results (reduce). This assumes the task decomposes cleanly and that the higher rate applies to the whole request.

column1: What is a sub-agent, and why are Haiku-class models a good fit for them?
column2: A cheap worker model that a larger planning model delegates small, well-defined tasks to (reading files, classifying, extracting). Most of an agent's tokens go through these calls, so low price and low latency matter most there.

column1: What's the status of Mistral Large 4 as of 2026-10-08?
column2: Public API preview since 2026-10-06. It has about 1T total and about 49B active parameters per token. Open weights are promised for late October (reports say 2026-10-27 or "end of month") but are not downloadable yet.

column1: What is the difference between an unattended agent like Stripe's Minions and a copilot?
column2: A copilot suggests code while a developer watches and accepts it. An unattended agent takes a task (for example from Slack), works alone in a sandbox, and returns a finished PR for human review.

column1: Why prefetch context with deterministic code instead of letting the agent look things up itself?
column2: It is cheaper and more predictable, and the model can't skip a step. Ordinary code gathers the ticket, thread and docs before the model runs.

column1: Why show an agent about 15 tools when 400+ exist?
column2: Too many tool definitions waste context and make the model pick badly. Selecting the relevant few per task improves reliability.

column1: Why do unattended agents run in sandboxes with no internet and no production data?
column2: So mistakes stay in a disposable environment, which makes it safe to run many agents in parallel and to let them execute commands without supervision.

column1: In an agent-plus-tests loop, what decides whether the work is done, and what should bound the loop?
column2: The real tests or CI decide, not the agent's claim of success. Cap the number of attempts, then hand off to a human.

column1: Why can a 90% per-token price cut still give only about 75% savings per task?
column2: Cost per task is price per token × tokens used. If the new model consumes more tokens per task, or requests land in a pricier tier, the savings shrink. Measure on your own workload.

column1: What is the cost-per-correct-answer metric, and why is it better than cost per call?
column2: Total cost divided by the number of correct answers. A cheap model that is wrong more often can cost more per correct result than it first appears, and a pricier one may cost less.

column1: What do Stripe's Minions have in common with the effort benchmark?
column2: Both rely on an objective check outside the model (CI tests, or a known-answer eval) rather than trusting the model's own claim of success.

column1: Name three dials that change what an LLM task costs.
column2: Model tier, reasoning effort, and request size (for example staying under Haiku 5.5's 100k-token tier boundary). Caching and output length also matter.

column1: Where does the model sit in a reliable unattended agent?
column2: In the middle of deterministic scaffolding: context is prefetched by ordinary code, only a few relevant tools are shown, it runs in a sandbox, and tests decide when it is done, with a capped retry loop.

column1: What are the three levels of getting JSON out of an LLM, from weakest to strongest?
column2: (1) Ask in the prompt and parse, with no guarantee. (2) JSON mode, which guarantees valid JSON in any shape. (3) Schema-enforced structured output, which guarantees valid JSON that matches your schema.

column1: Where does the schema go in the OpenAI Responses API and in the Claude Messages API?
column2: OpenAI: `text.format` with `type: "json_schema"`, `name`, `schema` and `strict: true`. Claude: `output_config.format` with `type: "json_schema"` and `schema`.

column1: What two schema rules do strict structured-output modes commonly require?
column2: Every object sets `additionalProperties: false`, and fields are listed as `required`. Make a field optional by allowing `null` as one of its types. Only a subset of JSON Schema is supported.

column1: What does a schema guarantee, and what doesn't it?
column2: It guarantees the output parses and has the right fields and types. It does not guarantee the values are correct, complete (truncation at `max_tokens`), or valid under business rules such as number ranges. Claude's structured outputs don't enforce numeric or string-length limits, so validate those in code.

column1: Why add an `"other"` or `"unknown"` value to an enum, and why put a `reasoning` field before `answer`?
column2: The escape hatch stops the model being forced into a wrong choice, which is the schema version of the "not found" rule. Fields are generated in order, so a reasoning field first lets the model think before it commits to the answer.

column1: Why does a schema-enforced eval measure model quality more cleanly than a prompt-and-parse eval?
column2: The schema guarantees every response parses and uses valid labels, so mistakes you see are wrong judgements, not formatting failures mixed into the score.

column1: Why should an eval count "failed" calls separately from "wrong" answers?
column2: Failures (truncation at `max_tokens`, refusals, exceptions) are usually config problems, while wrong answers are model-quality problems. Merging them hides which one to fix.

column1: What is cost per correct answer, and how is it computed in the harness?
column2: Total cost divided by the number of correct answers. Cost is summed per call as (input_tokens × input price + output_tokens × output price) / 1M, using `response.usage`.

column1: On Claude Haiku 5.5, why must `max_tokens` leave room beyond the visible JSON?
column2: Thinking is adaptive and on by default, and thinking tokens count toward the output limit and are billed as output. A low cap can truncate the response and make the call fail.

column1: What are the Python SDK entry points that return a typed object from a Pydantic model for Claude and for OpenAI's Responses API?
column2: Claude: `client.messages.parse(..., output_format=Model)` and read `parsed_output`. OpenAI: `client.responses.parse(..., text_format=Model)` and read `output_parsed`.

column1: What are the two Muse Wonder variants, and which one can you call through the API?
column2: Muse Wonder (`muse-wonder-1.0`) is on the Meta Model API, OpenRouter and Muse Code. Muse Wonder Full (`muse-wonder-full-1.0`) is only in the Muse Code Power and Max plans. Max reasoning effort on standard Wonder does not select Full.

column1: What are Muse Wonder's API price, context window and licence status?
column2: $4 per 1M input, $20 per 1M output and $0.20 per 1M cached input. The context window is 1,048,576 tokens with no long-context premium. Weights are not downloadable. Released 2026-10-12 and labelled a preview.

column1: Why is cached input especially important for a model like Muse Wonder?
column2: Long agent loops resend a growing prefix, so most input tokens can be cache hits. At $0.20 versus $4 per 1M, a cache hit costs 5% of the normal input price.

column1: How does Muse Wonder's pricing shape differ from Claude Haiku 5.5's?
column2: Wonder is flat at any context length. Haiku 5.5 charges $0.10 / $0.50 up to 100k tokens and $0.50 / $2.50 above that. Wonder costs more per token, but its cost grows in a straight line.

column1: What kind of workload is Muse Wonder aimed at, and what should you do before adopting it?
column2: Long-running agent work where the model plans, delegates to sub-agents, calls tools and recovers from errors, plus large multimodal prompts. Benchmark it on your own tasks using cost per correct answer, because most headline scores are vendor-reported and several are for the Full variant.

column1: What is the "gateway + act-as-user + audit log" pattern for agents?
column2: Every tool call the model proposes goes through one gateway. The gateway checks it against the permissions of the human who asked, enforces business rules in code, and logs the call and its outcome.

column1: Why should an agent act with the asking user's permissions instead of a shared admin account?
column2: The agent then can never do more than that user could do by hand. With a shared admin account, anyone who can talk to the agent effectively has admin rights.

column1: Why put a rule like "refunds over $100 need a human" in the gateway code and not only in the system prompt?
column2: A prompt rule is a request the model can ignore, misread, or be tricked out of. A code rule is enforced every time, whatever the model says.

column1: What should a gateway return when it denies a tool call?
column2: A clear error as the tool result, so the model can explain to the user or escalate to a human instead of crashing or retrying blindly.

column1: According to a 2026-10-07 secondary roundup, how does Airbnb give agents access to its trust systems, and how sure can you be of that?
column2: Reportedly MCP is the only path to about 10 trust systems, with logging and access control. It's unverified: the claim comes from a secondary summary, so check Airbnb's own write-up.
